question: As of January 2027, importers of oil and gas will be subject to new monitoring, reporting and verification requirements under Regulation (EU) 2024/1787 on the reduction of methane emissions. 17 Member States have reportedly warned that unclear compliance requirements and short deadlines for implementing these may lead suppliers to divert cargo outside the European Union.

The new obligations will come into effect during winter, when demand for gas and security of its supply are particularly important. The Commission was to suggest that, in the event of a threat to security of supply, Member States may temporarily refrain from imposing penalties while the legal obligations themselves remain in force. In view of this, I ask: 1.

Has the Commission assessed the risk of uncertainty associated with the new methane requirements coming into force in January 2027 leading to a reduction or redirection of gas supplies to the EU during the winter of 2026-2027, and what are the results of this assessment?
How does the Commission intend to ensure legal certainty for importers if obligations remain binding, while allowing Member States to refrain from imposing penalties for infringements?
Will the Commission consider postponing the application of the relevant import requirements until clear, enforceable and uniform compliance and verification rules are adopted?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.10.2026) According to Commission’s current assessment, the import requirements entering into force in January 2027 will not endanger security of energy supply in the EU. According to the Commission’s own assessment and recent independent studies1, global Oil & Gas Methane Partnership Level 5-compliant gas and oil volumes exceed current EU import needs.

On 20 July 2026, the Commission issued two recommendations to provide further clarity and legal certainty to Member States and market operators. The recommendation on compliance solutions2 provides clarity on how to demonstrate compliance with the import requirements, especially in complex supply chains.
The recommendation points out two solutions that already exist in the market, facilitating implementation for both industry and competent authorities.

To respond to the risks posed by tighter markets, the Commission also issued a recommendation for national competent authorities – who enforce the regulation, not to apply penalties3 on importers for a period lasting until 2029 so as to not endanger EU security of energy supply as referred to in Article 33(2) of the EU Methane Regulation4.

By clarifying the circumstances under which Article 33(2) of the Regulation provides for flexibility to implement the import requirements in a pragmatic manner, the latter recommendation contributes to legal certainty. The Commission cannot autonomously postpone the application and is not considering an amendment to the legal act.
